overview: Rain and high snow levels dominate the Pacific Northwest through Thursday, with cold air and snow arriving Friday. Western Wyoming and Montana get snow Friday into Saturday, while the Northeast sees mixed precipitation Friday before quieter, showery weather.

regions.title: Cascades
regions.text: Rain and strong winds lead the week, with snow levels high enough that the mountains see rain and snow mixed Wednesday through Thursday. Friday brings a shift to light snow, and Saturday is mostly quiet. Stevens Pass and Crystal Mountain both have 20" on the chart for the week, with the biggest day Wednesday. Mt. Baker is close behind.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Wet, mild weather dominates, with rain at times heavy Wednesday night and showers most days after. Whistler leads the region at 22" for the week, with its biggest day Wednesday. Snow is only likely near the peaks on Sunday night, as the rain line hangs on through the weekend.

regions.title: Northern Rockies
regions.text: Dry, mostly clear weather holds through Thanksgiving, with morning fog likely in the valleys. A system arrives Friday and brings snow to western Wyoming through Saturday, with a chance of snow east of the Divide Saturday. Jackson Hole leads at 8" on the chart. The NWS is calling for more, 12 to 25 inches Thursday night through Sunday night. Strong winds build along the Rocky Mountain Front before the snow arrives.

regions.title: Northeast
regions.text: Snow or rain returns Friday as the Thanksgiving storm passes north of the region, with strong winds and coastal flooding lingering into the weekend. A special weather statement covers Friday into Saturday. Le Massif leads with 9" for the week, most of it Thursday and Friday. Saturday and Sunday turn showery, with flurries or rain at times.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 11, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Nov 22–28. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
